Just Story 6 min read · Oct 2, 2026 -- Listen Share Choose according to the buyer’s route, the delivery requirements, and the work you can maintain. Press enter or click to view image in full size You can compare Etsy and Gumroad fees for an hour and still avoid the most important question: how will someone find this particular product? A platform can provide a suitable checkout while leaving the acquisition problem unresolved. It can also expose a product to relevant searches while placing it among many competing offers. The better launch choice depends on the product and the route to its first buyers. Start there before building two stores. Should a beginner choose Etsy or Gumroad? Etsy is a reasonable candidate when the product fits its rules and buyers already search the marketplace for that kind of item. Gumroad is a reasonable candidate when you can bring suitable visitors through content, recommendations, an existing audience, or another identifiable source. These are starting points, not guarantees. Etsy does not promise traffic because you publish a listing. Gumroad also has a discovery system, but a new seller must account for its eligibility requirements rather than assuming it will produce the first sale. Gumroad’s Discover requirements The practical question is which platform fits the purchase journey you can realistically support. Check the basic requirements before comparing features First, confirm that the product is eligible and that you can operate an account with a supported payout setup. Do this using the current platform documentation for your circumstances. Product eligibility can eliminate an option before the fee comparison begins. For example, Etsy’s current standards exclude AI prompt bundles. Etsy’s Creativity Standards Next, inspect the delivery. What files does the buyer receive? How large are they? Does the product need several editions, a license choice, ongoing updates, or a setup process? Write down those requirements independently of either platform. This prevents you from treating an awkward workaround as a product requirement simply because you started building the listing in one place. A platform is a poor fit when delivering the promised experience requires repeated explanations, fragile links, or manual corrections you cannot reliably maintain. Map the purchase journey in one paragraph Describe where the buyer starts, what they want, what they see before the product page, and what evidence helps them decide. For a printable, the journey might begin with a specific marketplace search and a comparison of thumbnails. For a developer resource, it might begin with a technical article, a working demonstration, and a link to the complete kit. Those journeys create different demands. The search-led product needs language and images that make sense beside competing listings. The article-led product needs a convincing connection between the useful content and the paid deliverable. Neither route is automatically easier. One depends more heavily on marketplace matching and presentation. The other requires a credible way to distribute content or recommendations. If you cannot describe either journey clearly, opening an additional store is unlikely to resolve the problem. Work on the route to the buyer first. Scenario 1: A printable people already search for Imagine a seller creating an original moving checklist for renters. The format is straightforward, and the seller finds relevant marketplace searches and comparable products. Etsy may be a sensible first test because the product matches a recognizable shopping behavior. The work still includes choosing an accurate title, presenting the pages clearly, explaining the digital format, and showing why the checklist fits this particular use. The seller should inspect the competition for practical differences. Perhaps the product organizes tasks around notice dates, packing, utilities, and move-out documentation in a way the target buyer can use. That difference must be visible. A generic printable entering a crowded result set does not become distinctive merely because the marketplace has shoppers. Gumroad could also deliver the same product, but the seller would need a plausible route to visitors, such as a useful moving guide with an appropriate audience. The product’s simplicity does not remove the acquisition requirement. Scenario 2: A technical resource demonstrated through content Now imagine a creator selling a source-code starter kit. The buyer needs to understand supported environments, installation steps, included functionality, and what they will need to customize. A tutorial or demonstration may be central to the decision. If the creator can publish a credible explanation of the technical problem and show the kit running, Gumroad may fit the route from content to checkout. The product page can continue the explanation with requirements, screenshots, contents, and license details. The work does not end at the sale.
